story_text.value:
Hey HN, I built Emittr because, i frequently deal with air-gapped or locked-down systems where USB storage is disabled and third party software cannot be installed. Nobody blocks a physical keyboard, so i used the Linux Kernel's USB gadget subsystem (ConfigFS at /dev/hidg0) to turn a rooted android phone to a real USB HID Keyboard and mouse. 1. No installation on target device. It talks to motherboard USB controller, so it works in every locked down OS as well, BIOS, GRUB, etc. 2. Out of band bridge : we don't store passwords or authenticators on rooted phone. Emittr exposes a web UI on LAN, so we can send keystrokes from our main phones. 3. Types long scripts (chatgpt debuggings), SSH keys or passwords at ~1000 WPM without touching the host's clipboard. 4. OS can see this only as a genuine HID keyboard/mouse. Zero host footprint as no drivers, software or background scripts on target machine. 5. Uses USB-IF 0x0238 via on-screen joysticks instead of synthetic Shift + Scroll hacks.

Feel free to check the work and try if you have a rooted android handy. GitHub: https://github.com/mr-anjaneyam/Emittr Webpage: https://emittr.srianjaneyam.me/

I'm planning to record and add few demos in various scenarios (Windows, macOS, android, linux, bios) and devices (Phone, PC, TV, STB, Kiosk).

Happy to answer any questions and would love to hear your suggestions, feature ideas or edge cases.

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I'm James, one of the co-founders of Coral.

Coral is an open-source, self-hosted gateway that sits between your agents and the systems they work on. Agents call tools by writing short TypeScript programs that they can save as custom tools to reuse.

You can publish custom tools for groups of agents, so your team’s library of tools adapts to your unique systems, data and use cases. Custom tools help agent performance and give more precise units of permission control.

Here’s a short demo: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p0PKOlHLyVI

We started on this while building an AI SRE. To investigate an incident, the agent had to connect the dots across an ocean of telemetry data and undocumented relationships across internal and external systems. It took broad permissions, a lot of tokens and it would start from scratch the next time.

We built Coral so that the agent remembers the route. Once a task succeeds, the agent writes the steps that worked into a program and saves it as a custom tool. Next time, the agent finds that custom tool in the same search as standard provider tools (e.g. Datadog, Slack), and reuses it. It started with SRE, but we (and our early users) now use Coral for agent work across the org.

For our tasks across GitHub, Linear and Slack with Opus 5.5, custom tools help agents work 29% faster, at 31% lower cost (tasks here: https://withcoral.com/docs/examples/custom-tools).

Coral builds on code mode, adding custom tools, policy controls and managed identities. Each program runs in a V8 isolate with no network access or credentials. Coral checks every tool call against workspace policy before attaching credentials and forwarding it to the provider. You can configure each provider to use the caller’s own account, so teammates can share tools without sharing API tokens. (e.g. https://withcoral.com/blog/slackbot-works-better-with-coral)

Coral is written in Rust, and you can run it as a desktop app or as a shared server. The core is Apache 2.0 and has no limits on users, agents or volume. Everything I've described here is in the OSS edition. SAML, SCIM, and org-wide governance features will be available soon under an enterprise licence.

We'd love for you to try it and share your feedback. You can download it here https://withcoral.com/download.

I'll be in the comments here and on Slack: https://withcoral.com/slack

story_text.value:
I've been working on Claktor ever since I got frustrated with some 'code smells' AI Agents have been producing while writing Rust. Claktor is a refactoring tool that leverages custom AST parsing and processing to produce ranked 'leads' on what in the codebase should be looked into to reduce logic duplication. When I started out, it was mostly an opinionated 'how code should be written' detector, after attempting to formalize something objectively useful out of it I've arrived to this.

How is it scored? When exploring how to try to roughly judge how much logic there is in a program, the first approach is LOC. However that is just a proxy as lines can have lots of meat and can be gamed. What we arrived to are 'normalized tokens' which is a parsing of a normalized program by an LLM tokenizer. This neatly fits into then cost of reading the modified file by AI Agents. The more normalized tokens we reduce while preserving behaviour, the more deduplicated to codebase is and cheaper it is to read, extend, test and maintain by AI Agents. (the normalization is subject to some guards like: removing types does not reduce tokens)

Is this developed to the extent that it can be? By all means no! It already is very effective however as it greedily ranks everything through the codebase so AI Agents can remove around 3 to 10 times more for the same cost depending on the repo.

Please try it out and let me know how it goes! Currently works with TS,JS,Rust and Python

story_text.value:
I wanted a good Python dead code finder that just works, with minimal config, until Ruff adds support for that (https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/issues/872).

None of the newer alternatives to Vulture worked out of the box on my codebases, so I decided to build one.

The first version was in Python, then I switched to Rust for speed and to reuse Ruff's parser. It checks all of CPython in under a second.

It found lots of interesting dead code in my team's codebases, and it's the first time in years we've had a Python dead code finder in our CI.

Feedback is very welcome, especially dead code it misses.

title.value: Show HN: Unref – A Python dead code finder built on Ruff's parser

story_text.value:
This started out as a casual side project, tinkering with AI to play some of my favorite old adventure games like King's Quest and Space Quest in the browser. Now it's a self-running, self-maintaining, self-iterating side project capable of importing, playing (single player or multiplayer), or modding those games (manually or with AI), or creating completely new games from scratch. It sort of invented a couple of its own "languages" along the way? It calls one of them the "machine form" which is in the ballpark of LLVM IR and ghidra p-code, and the other one is a TypeScript subset, meant to be a more human-readable layer on top of the machine form. Honestly I'm still trying to catch up a bit on what it's done and continuing to do.

I linked to the "Making Of" page of the app because I think my process and "collaboration" with Claude might actually be even more interesting than the project itself.

As a software engineer, I've been grappling with how to use or not use AI in this new world we're living in. Here's my most optimistic attitude after working on this project:

- Coding before AI was more like building with legos, one piece at a time.

- Coding with AI is more like sculpting, where you already start with material, and you shape and shave and chip off what you don't like until you get something closer to what you want.

For this project, I provided (and sometimes continue to tweak) the main goal and vision. At the beginning I still kicked off each Claude session myself and was actively prompting each step. At some point though, enough documentation had been made that my sessions started becoming one prompt of "what's next" and then a second prompt of "ok, go". So now I have an "ops coordinator" Claude session that runs routinely and spins up additional Claude sessions to keep working on the project...without me. They do things like work through the queue of already-planned work, brainstorm new items to work on, test existing work, do research into related projects or applications, have meetings with each other, and propose new directions or breaking changes to me. If there's something that requires me, I get notified. There are also several Claude html artifacts that function as a a sort of dashboard that I can pull up to see what's been done recently, what's coming up next, and what questions or action items there are for me.

Even though that sounds very hands-off, I find that I'm actually still pretty involved, because I like to redirect and nudge what the agents are working on pretty frequently. And that process does still feel pretty creative and engaging. Hence my "sculpting" attitude.

But, there are other possible metaphors for coding with AI that also come to mind...

- IKEA

- Frankenstein

So at this point, I guess it's still an open question: is what I'm making more of a sculpted work of art, or more like Frankenstein's monster?

story_text.value:
Hi HN,

I’m Kevin, I run product at PrettyWhale.ai, a small team based in France.

We've spent the last few months building a VS Code extension that writes the tedious part of ingestion code from a data sample.

How it works: You give it a CSV or JSON sample. It profiles the fields, you pick the ones to keep, then it suggests transformations you can accept, edit or drop. At the end you get a complete Python project in your workspace that includes all the necessary quality controls: - Pipeline & transformation code - Unit tests - Config files - Documentation

A design choice we care about: the generation of pipeline is driven by a deterministic workflow rather than an endless chat window (no prompting required). We truly believe that the future of integrating AI into tools will involve a redesign of our user interfaces to get the most out of it.

What it doesn’t do yet: it works from a file (CSV or JSON) you already have. It doesn’t connect to databases or API. These features are scheduled for release by the end of the year.

To try it, there’s a VS Code extension: https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=prettywh... You need an account but free with no credit card.

The model runs on our servers, and the samples are not used to train the models.

title.value: Show HN: Prettywhale.ai – Generate data pipelines from data samples

story_text.value:
Hi, I'm Max. I've used many hosts file switchers over the years to do local development with real hostnames/domains, combined with HTTPS reverse-proxies.

I made HostsTray to combine both into one tool.

Through a tray icon (Windows) or menu bar (macOS) you can toggle groups of hosts file entries, and toggle the HTTPS proxy.

The HTTPS proxy first installs a local CA cert into your keychain/certificate store, and then uses it to create certificates for each domain that passes through the proxy.

You can configure the proxy to route different paths to different ports locally. Websockets are also supported.

A common problem when editing hosts file is to make Chrome/other browser actually update the DNS cache. I found this is due to Chrome holding a pool of open connections in the background. HostsTray solves this by dropping the open connections to addresses that changed, forcing Chrome to reconnect and re-lookup the hostnames. It is VERY satisfying to toggle a hosts group and see Chrome obey immediately.

Switching can be password-free using an optional helper that runs as admin. The helper only does switching/toggling of groups you already have.

HostsTray also exposes a local API to toggle hosts groups and the proxy. The API also serves a skill suitable for coding agents. So you can let Claude Code toggle for you. It can also add new hostnames to HostsTray, but that requires user verification from you.

The whole thing is a ~10 MB binary written in Go, open-source for Windows and macOS.

Hope this can be useful Feedback is very welcome.
